interactions.summary: Jiang and Sneako clarify that Larry Fink himself promoted the DEI turn and is now publicly treating it as a failed experiment that capital can move past.
Jiang says Fink and allied institutions pushed DEI as a response to Occupy Wall Street, turning attention away from class unity.
Sneako agrees, restating the logic as divide-and-conquer to stop the 99 percent from uniting against the 1 percent.
Jiang compresses the argument into the line that unity has become intolerable to corporate power.
Sneako pivots back to AI by asking Jiang to explain how AI becomes profitable only when it 'becomes God' and why he links that to antichrist or data-religion themes.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang calls Larry Fink "chairman of the world economic forum," which may reflect a loose or mistaken institutional title in speech; the packet preserves the claim as spoken rather than normalizing it.
The phrase rendered as "pushed the eye" is contextually a reference to DEI, and "as responsible to occupy wall street" appears to mean as a response to Occupy Wall Street.
Sneako paraphrases Jiang's earlier lecture language about AI, antichrist, and data as God. This is a setup question, not yet Jiang's answer to those terms within this packet.

claims.claim: Jiang says Larry Fink was one of the main elite figures who pushed DEI politics before later treating them as expendable.
He argues that DEI politics were pushed by elite institutions in order to redirect or fracture the class solidarity signaled by Occupy Wall Street.
The exchange converges on the idea that elite cultural politics function by preventing the 99 percent from uniting against the 1 percent.
Jiang states that unity is now treated as a threat by corporate America.
Sneako frames Jiang's AI thesis as saying the technology is currently expensive and unprofitable but could become profitable if it matures into a quasi-religious or total social authority.
claims.temporal_scope: Interviewer summary of Jiang's earlier position, restated on 2026-05-18 as a setup question.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang boils the whole anti-solidarity argument down to a single dirty word.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Unity is the dirtiest word in corporate America right now
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's strongest reusable line and a compact lens for his claim that elite culture management exists to prevent mass alignment.

signature_moments.moment: The conversation pivots from class fragmentation to AI theology by making profitability dependent on becoming God.
signature_moments.source_phrase: AI is not profitable until it becomes God
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Even though Sneako is asking the question, the line marks the threshold into one of Jiang's most charged AI formulations and sets up the next packet's answer.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang treats unity not as a civic good but as the specific social condition corporate power most needs to prevent, because united majorities could target elite control directly.
Sneako's summary phrase for the elite tactic Jiang is endorsing: splitting possible class solidarity into competing identity fragments so coordinated resistance never forms.

chronology_notes.note: The packet closes the DEI-versus-Occupy explanation by condensing it into the anti-unity line, then immediately uses that ideological frame as a launch point into Jiang's AI-as-God argument in the next packet.

uncertainty_notes.note: Sneako's summary that Fink called DEI a failed experiment is part of the interviewer's paraphrase in this packet and is not independently substantiated here beyond the participants' exchange.
